items.title: [apnews.com] European-Japanese BepiColombo enters Mercury orbit ahead of two-probe science mission
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, entered orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21, completing an eight-year journey and becoming the second mission to orbit the planet. The two orbiters remain attached; they are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10 and take up different polar orbits, with science operations due to begin in April 2027. The mission will use the European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, called Mio, to study Mercury from separate vantage points. Their instruments are designed to examine the planet’s surface and interior, its magnetic field and the thin gas envelope around it, including how the magnetic field interacts with the solar wind. Controllers in Germany confirmed the spacecraft’s capture several hours after a series of braking thruster firings, with the spacecraft about 152 million kilometers away. A propulsion-system problem delayed BepiColombo’s arrival from December 2025. Its nominal science mission is planned to last one Earth year, with an extension through 2029.

items.title: [physicsworld.com] Scientists propose supercritical fluids drove deep Mariana volcanic eruptions
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers propose that supercritical water in magma could explain how volcanic deposits formed more than 6,000 meters down the Mariana Trench wall, building on the discovery of unusually deep pyroclastic rocks. At those pressures, water behaves neither like an ordinary liquid nor a gas and expands far less than steam. The team says this may have enabled magma to fragment without the force of a land eruption. The mechanism remains uncertain: researchers have not found the vents or directly observed an eruption. Rock samples contain “double breccia,” suggesting two closely spaced episodes of fracturing — one possibly linked to supercritical fluid and another to its conversion to steam at the seafloor. The team plans further analysis of the volcanic material and aims to explore farther along the plate boundary. Jason/Medea cannot descend below 6,500 meters, short of the Challenger Deep floor at about 11,000 meters.

items.content_html:

A study published in *Nature Astronomy* suggests that a stretch of the Milky Way’s Norma arm traced by masers may instead be a star-forming shock front along the leading edge of the galaxy’s central bar. The University of Sydney-led team reached that interpretation by comparing galaxy simulations with existing maser measurements; it did not directly image the shock front or collect new observations. The researchers say the result concerns only the maser segment near the bar’s end, not the entire Norma-Outer arm, and requires further investigation.

items.title: [theguardian.com] European-Japanese BepiColombo prepares to enter Mercury orbit after eight years
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is due to enter orbit around Mercury on Nov. 21 after an eight-year journey of about 6 billion miles, becoming only the second mission to orbit the planet. Its two orbiters will investigate Mercury’s surface, interior and magnetic environment, including its unusually large metal core, the origins of its magnetic field and ice in permanently shadowed craters. A propulsion-system problem delayed BepiColombo’s arrival, and reaching Mercury requires careful braking against the Sun’s gravity. The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter will map the surface’s composition and study the interior; Japan’s orbiter will measure the magnetic field and the planet’s thin sodium exosphere. The spacecraft are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with science operations planned to begin in April 2027.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Chile's Rubin Observatory survey could test hidden planet theory
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Chile’s Vera C. Rubin Observatory is conducting a decade-long survey that could help astronomers test whether distant icy bodies follow orbital patterns predicted for a hypothetical planet beyond Neptune. Its expanding catalogue will provide more objects to compare, but detecting the planet itself would be much harder because it would appear extremely faint. An international team led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka, a researcher at Japan’s Kindai University, used simulations of 4.5 billion years of Solar System evolution to propose Planet X2 as a possible explanation for some distant objects’ unusual orbits. Astronomers have not observed the planet, and the model does not match every feature of the known objects’ orbital distribution.

Results reported Nov. 16 from two phase 3 trials showed substantial reductions in body mass index (BMI) with semaglutide in children aged 6 to 11 with obesity and tirzepatide in adolescents aged 12 to 17. After 68 weeks, children receiving semaglutide had a 13.5% BMI decrease, compared with a 2.7% increase among those receiving placebo; in the 72-week teen trial, tirzepatide produced a 19-percentage-point greater BMI reduction than placebo. Both studies also recorded improvements in cardiometabolic measures, while gastrointestinal side effects were common. In the semaglutide trial, BMI began rising during a seven-week washout after treatment stopped. Ania Jastreboff, a Yale obesity researcher, said results from 26 weeks off treatment are expected in the coming months.

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [phys.org] Deep-sea robot finds deepest volcanic deposits near Challenger Deep
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea has found what researchers describe as the deepest documented underwater pyroclastic deposits, on the Mariana Trench wall about 6,000 meters below sea level. The rocks provide evidence of volcanic flows in the trench’s western forearc, where geologists expected little volcanic activity because the mantle is generally not hot enough to melt. The findings were published Nov. 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science. The team’s observations support the idea that the Pacific Plate bends steeply as it sinks beneath the Mariana plate. That could help explain Challenger Deep’s depth and bring magma-generating processes closer to the trench. But researchers have not identified the eruption sites or established how eruptions could produce these deposits under immense water pressure. They say further sampling and radiometric dating are needed. Jason/Medea cannot reach the seafloor below 6,500 meters, while Challenger Deep extends to about 11,000 meters.

items.title: [healio.com] Children with atopic dermatitis show higher odds of sleep disturbance
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Children and young adults with atopic dermatitis had 28% higher odds of sleep disturbance than peers without the condition, a retrospective review of 26,395 patients at an urban primary care clinic found. The association remained after researchers accounted for coexisting atopy and mental health conditions; neither significantly changed the link. The study included patients aged 0 to 21; 14.5% had atopic dermatitis and 10.3% had sleep disturbance. Samantha Sundermeier, DO, an attending physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, said future studies should assess disease severity, treatment response and sleep over time using validated measures and patient-reported outcomes.

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Study links very large and small waists to higher death risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A study of more than 17 million South Korean adults found that both unusually large and unusually small waist measurements were associated with a higher risk of death across weight and age groups. The lowest observed risk was associated with waist circumferences of 80–94 centimeters in men and 75–89 centimeters in women. The association between waist circumference and death risk was stronger at older ages, especially among women 75 and older. Researchers analyzed routine health-check measurements from 2009–10 and tracked survival for nearly 14 years, through June 30, 2024. The study was observational and cannot show that waist size causes death. Among people with normal weight or overweight whose waist circumference was high for their body mass index (BMI), reducing waist circumference without necessarily losing weight appeared to offer a greater survival benefit than losing weight while reducing waist circumference, the authors said.

Southern California also faces high tides and surf, after October flooding damaged 114 homes and other structures in Huntington Beach alone. Forecasters expect hazardous coastal conditions to persist through the week; further king tides are forecast for Dec. 23–25 and Jan. 21–22.

items.title: [energytracker.asia] COP31 fossil-fuel deadlock leaves energy shift to voluntary pledges
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after the European Union and several other countries rejected a draft that omitted a direct reference to moving away from fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil-fuel-dependent states opposed such language. Delegates adopted no new overarching political direction on fossil fuels, while separate voluntary initiatives continued, including an electrification pledge backed by more than 90 countries. A proposal to expand carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne scale by 2035 was also disputed. Global operating capture capacity was about 68 million tonnes a year in mid-2026, while deployment across Asia remains limited. Countries adopted a three-year extension of the Just Transition Work Programme, but the mechanism intended to put it into operation remained underdeveloped. The International Maritime Organization’s 176 member states are due to discuss a shipping emissions framework on Nov. 30 that could establish global carbon pricing and binding measures.

Investors at a closed-door meeting said climate finance needs private capital, but some asset owners remain cautious about emerging-market projects because they lack reliable ways to assess and manage the risks. Developing countries including India are pressing for clearer obligations and more adaptation funding, while the European Union favors using existing finance mechanisms rather than creating a new work program. Outside the talks, organizers said more than 10,000 people joined a Nov. 14 climate march calling for grants, support for affected communities and a transition away from fossil fuels. Negotiators have a 104-paragraph climate-finance draft, released Nov. 14, and are due to continue discussions on finance and a just transition in the summit’s second week.

items.title: [frontpageafricaonline.com] COP31 draft proposes $120 billion in annual adaptation finance by 2035
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A draft COP31 agreement proposes at least $120 billion a year in adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, alongside accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20. African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

Per Strand, who heads two of the regulatory groups, warned that a nationwide blackout could affect all nine operating reactors simultaneously and urged European countries to coordinate emergency preparations if attacks continue. Residents travelled by bus through occupied Crimea to Russia, then flew to Belarus and crossed into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, where relatives and aid workers met them. Russia’s human rights commissioner said both sides had agreed to continue humanitarian missions. The truce was set to expire Sunday night.
